review_text_raw:
I really wanted to give this a positive review, as someone who loves games like this ( Papers Please! being a personal favorite)

However, I'm very indifferent due to the lack of content and the seemingly linear focus of the story and the severe lack of challenge ( all your options are highlighted for you)

It had a TON of potential and did give a very 1984ish vibe, and I enjoyed the small amounts of content it offered ( 30 minutes an episode?). However if you, like me, go into this expecting a Papers Please! experience you will be severely disappointed.

5/10 ( don't buy unless it is on sale is my reccomendation -- or until all episodes have been unlocked for one continuous playthrough)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I expected to have to do more "detective work", but this is just a choices-don't-make-sense-but-they-matter experience.  Especially in the final chapter, I had little clue what I was supposed to accomplish, and then suddenly I accomplished something and the game was over.

If I could give this a Thumbs-Sideways, I would.  There are a few interesting "scenes" and moments that were surprising, but as it stands, I didn't feel like I was enjoying myself.  Just uploading "datachunks" and waiting for the game to find more datachunks to be uploaded.  Occasionally I had to decide between two conflicting pieces of data, but those choices were less-than-half of the game.  Maybe one-third of the game is "decisions" like that, and the rest is just dragging datachunks from one side of the screen to the other.  Or in some cases, deciding NOT to drag a datachunk from one side of the screen to the other, because it might be misunderstood by your superiors. For example, one comment on a website in-game says "oh no! the torture! ;)" in a playful manner about being bribed with muffins, but if you upload it your boss takes it to mean LITERAL TORTURE and freaks out about it.  So you're told to upload "all the relevant data" but then have no say in how it gets interpreted or used, which impacts upon the relevance of said data.

If you like games that try to make political-statements about things, this is probably up your alley.  I just wanted to solve puzzles, connect clues, etc.  The game highlights all the relevant information, and then connects it to things for you.  Not TERRIBLE, but not what I expected or hoped for. :(

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm stopping because of the mechanic: Conflicted Datachunks.

You're presented two conflicting stories and have to choose which is true.  It's fun when you can figure out why the stories conflict. Most of the time, though, there's not enough evidence.  And once you make a choice - there's no going back.

This is opposite of how we should handle conflictings ideas. It's important to avoid jumping to conclusions - something your counterpart Symes does consistently. It's important to be open to possibilities and revise your position if new valid evidence comes in.

We're all subject to confirmation bias - games can teach us how to recognize and manage it.  "Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments" is a better model for dealing with difficult, uncertain decisions.

I'm happy Osmotic Studios is tackling such weighty topics in their games, but it also means the skills the player practices need to build solid foundations for dealing with those issues.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

review_text_raw:
I am a huge computer sim detective game fan. I love games like Cyber Manhunt 1/2, Simulacra 1/2, Greyhat, etc. Orwell is one I have tried a couple times to get into... but it's just so boring to me.

Most importantly, the gameplay. I never feel like I am actually solving a puzzle, but instead just reading and deciding on a handful of choose your own adventure type choices. Nothing you do seems to matter, and ever answer is already highlighted for you, It just feels like a visual novel.

But also - the story is so boring. The 1984 sureveillance angle has been done to death, and this just feels like nothing new. I genuinely am surprised so many people seem to enjoy this game. To me, it just has nothing to offer.

review_text_raw:
I've been hesitating writing a review for this one, as part of me likes the game but another part is very annoyed with it. After giving it some rest and extra thought, I have to downvote it.

The gameplay is fine, I actually quite liked that. The concept works and I would have loved a much more difficult version using this technique.

Sadly, the story is very flawed and made in such a way to get the game's "message" out. It is very biased towards why all this is a bad idea and pretty much gives no indication why and how it could actually work. And you know, that all would have been fine if done right, but everything in the story hinges on a lot of coincidences and it takes away from how an actual Orwell system could maybe properly work.

It still wouldn't, but this case does not show the actual flaws of such a system. And that is the problem of this game. It starts off by you following ONE suspect. In a true case you would have had information on everyone at the crime scene, and this is only the first big flaw why this is a bad representation of a system like this. [spoiler]And then that suspect ends up not being involved at all, but by coincidence she does happen to be in contact with the true criminal. Oh, sure, the writers eventually tried to make a link and explain it was the criminal who was responsible for the first suspect to be a the crime scene. Which ends up with the story making even less sense as there is absolutely no indication why the criminal would even want this suspect to be at the first crime scene.[/spoiler] And it just goes downhill from there, with more random stuff happening that just happens to be convenient for this poor mirror or a true spying system.

Conclusion: Good concept, but the writing keeps it from being a good game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]English:[/b]
The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

そしてOrwellでは“ハイライトされている情報だけ”が利用可能なのですが、例えば関係者の画像を見付けたから登録したいと思ってもハイライトされていないなら使えない――と思いきや後になって急にハイライトされるという事も。つまりシステム(進行度等)の都合で意味の有無が一転してしまうので「役に立つか分からないが留めておきたい」みたいな遊び方は全く想定されておらず、“調査官”という言葉から連想して捜査・整理・推理というパズル的な喜びを期待すると肩透かしを食らいます。

Orwellを通じた通話や情報端末への無許可でのアクセスは人権や倫理への一種の加害性というディストピアがディストピアたる所以を描写してはいますが、プレイヤーの視点では上記の通り(=重要人物以外には触れられない) 犯罪や危機の捜査にしか使われておらず、しかも問題となる事件が死傷者を伴うテロなので、倫理観を脇に置くのは超法規的措置だと補完する事も出来てしまう。
その犯人がOrwellを非難したところで犠牲者を生んだテロリストの言説として空虚に響くだけでしょう。

review_text_clean: [b]English:[/b] The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.” You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when. Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there. Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked. Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon. The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize. Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue. And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place? I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it. Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the story is interesting and I can see replayability in knowing you've made the wrong move, then creating a new profile and trying to avoid that scenario... I haven't done that. I probably won't either, because I have to agree with other players: the game guides you too much.

You're basically told where to click and when, which completely defeats the point of having all of these fun tools at your disposal--they might as well have dumped all data pieces in a list and had you click on them one by one, all after the other.

The auto-highlighting spoils the point of reading anything. The game warns you that potential choices conflict instead of letting the player decide on how thoroughly they want to investigate before submitting information. Some pieces of info feel completely useless, but your supervisor somehow decides they have more value than they should and the supervisor's decision often feels like a complete whim. And vice-versa: bits of info you feel should be important are locked away or not even meant to be accessible because the game decided "Nope, I won't even let you go into that dead-end for fun".

I guess this was worth what I paid for it... $2! and no more. This had a lot of promise but it doesn't have enough depth or freedom of choice for my tastes.

review_text_raw:
Short and simple.
It has a very enjoyible narrative where you play as a sort of detective.
Gameplay is limited by rules that are stated in the begining. 

Some more information?
The game is designed for the curious and detective types to search through forums, profiles, live text channels, and police reports to figure out who and why the cause of horrible events happen.
However you can also just as effectively "play" the game by scrolling through the pages only looking for the light-blue highlighted words to which you click and drag to the left on the profiles. For live chat rooms, you can just wait for information to show up that is able to be clicked on. The only time where you make a true decision is if you find yellow-highlighted text that contridicts information located somewhere else.

As a narrative experience for those who want to relax back and feel part of the story, this game is fantastic for you.
 For those who thought this would be a Challenging experience will be dissatisfied by simplistic gameplay of clicking and dragging.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Lot of good, but outweighed by the bad.

The game was entertaining and built on a thought-provoking premise, but the game is far too short (roughly four hours in length) and the premise of the game loses its edge when the game picks a side on the question if society should sacrifice privacy for security instead of leaving that decision up to the player.

The story is well-written but offers very little in replayability. The games premise would have room for several scenarios where the player has to puzzle together what has happened or attempt to prevent crimes from happening, placing the player in situations where he has to weigh his decision how deep into someones private-life he should go to discover the truth, and even then be left with an uncertainty that forces him to make decisions based only his own interpretation of the truth. Instead, the game presents one scenario that plays out over a five-day period. The game-mechanics themselves are not complicated and the games graphics and presentation is mostly text and still-pictures, so more scenarios should not be difficult or time-consuming to add later on.

If the game had more meat on the bones I would recommend it, but for the moment this is a brief game with little replayability, but potential for a lot more.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Short version: makes you do Important Choices With Consequences based on very little, very shaky, third hand info. Not fun or challenging or possible to engage with sincerely.

Long version: early in the first ep, during what you might call the tutorial, you are asked to choose between two versions of the truth: that a crime suspect was released and case closed because of A) lack of evidence or B) bribes. You are given no context for this choice other than a news article stating that the official version is A but some people think it might be B. I'm not exaggerating. All you have to go on is the word of a journalist you don't know, reporting the words of other people you don't know regarding an incident you just heard of. Even so the game stresses that anything you report will be taken as The Truth and there will be no possibility to undo the choice.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" seems content to repeat what books and movies have said more eloquently.  It also falls below the dollar per hour metric (it can be completed within 5 hours).

The gameplay is simple and involves clicking through fake internet websites, blogs, and chat logs to collect bits of information (a process that can easily become tedious).

So the appeal is obviously the story, but for $9.99, you're better off buying a copy of George Orwell's 1984, or Aldous Huxley's Brave New World instead. This game is nothing more than a shallow summary of the themes explored in depth by those literary works.

Unity engine build: 2018.3.0f2. There were some graphical issues with the native Linux version. Solved by using Proton.

Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

I don't feel like I can truly call this a detective game, or even a puzzle game. The choices available are limited (2-3 outcomes), and [spoiler] almost none of the choices that are made throughout the game affect the ending, or really the flow of the story in general[/spoiler]. How exactly does the investigator incriminating oneself IMMEDIATELY result in the termination of Orwell? How does an incredibly sophisticated surveillance program like Orwell, even still in test phase, get torn down in a day? Never mind that there were probably backup investigators lined up, or that The Party likely would not have wanted to let go of the project so easily. And yet curtail in an instant, they did. [/spoiler]

Credit where it is due, the character dialogue and writings felt very genuine, and portrayed each person convincingly.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I hesitated before giving the thumb down to a game which is not completely bad, but definitely not for everyone.
The game basically plays like a visual story where you have to grab (drag  & drop more exactly) chunks of data to the left of the screen on the right character, the interface is not perfect (no right clicking to add intel faster, some back buttons are just visuals). The game is SLOW and a bit boring if you play in one go, no way to speed up text, no voice acting, forces you to wait on a few occasions. 
The writing isn't bad but characters lack personnality (bit shallow, not enough background), the game forces you to go one way and lacks some imaginative gameplay (older games would have make you work with visual clues, make interrogation yourself but Orwell keeps making you reading text). The problem is that it plays like a slow VN where you have to constantly look for the next button without any way to speed things up. 
It's not overly long but it feels long and the whole debate it's supposed to bring up falls a bit flat, also you can guess the "responsible person" before the end as soon as some intel is revealed. 
The game offers several ends but does not warn you before making the final choice (it did force you to watch a wall of text on an ugly colored screen before though) and would force you to replay from scratch to make another choice.

Don't mistaken me, those who are in for a lengthy text experience set in the modern world with text centered spying are in for a treat but it's definitely not for everyone.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really want to like Orwell for the principle of trying to deliver a social media exploitation simulator, but ultimately, it's a flow-chart puzzle that only allows the player to progress once he or she has collected the necessary datachunks. This would be unobtrusive if the narrator (the guide) wasn't hovering over you at all times like an incompetent manager - instantly responding with positive or negative feedback. The game would be much better if you could upload information to something like a holding pool to review as a whole before submitting it to something like a file or record for the manager to review, but instead, the game flow pauses and continues with no continuity of real-time, even though the game desperately tries to emulate this moment of your day on the job . You might have a hunch about a suspect as you read information, so you would think to point out correlated characteristics, but nope, that doesn't matter because you can only upload information the game has already marked as valid.

Orwell is unique and immersive, so it does have that going for it, but the flow-chart progression heavily relies on the game being bug free. I hit a bug/glitch/design flaw in the second episode in which a datachunk in the suspects relationship field was not registering that I uploaded it. As a result, I was stuck. I poured over every bit of information for about three hours before I finally searched online for help and wound up uploading conflicting datachunks to do what I thought would fail the mission, but oh, how convenient, the game saves the day by holding my hand and progressing anyway. So, it’s more like an interactive novel than a social-engineering investigation simulator.

Yes you get an "adviser" that hovers over your shoulder making wise-crack comments and wild accusations for data that you are harvesting, Symes is the ideal state bureaucrat that everybody loves to hate.

George Orwell is spinning in his grave.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell is basically just working but with more steps. Thankfully I got it on sale, but I wouldn’t recommend it as I felt I was just doing admin work the whole time. Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A dire and very timely warning, the game takes places in a fictional country where the government is adopting more and more authoritarian and - well, Orwellian - methods of surveillance and control. You're recruited by the eponymous government agency that is in charge of combating crime, and your handling of emerging evidence determines if you contribute to the country's descent into a police state or not.  

I liked the premise, but I found it all a bit too caricatured, although the game switches things up by presenting an alternate contemporary reality where the authoritarian push comes from the other side. 

Most of all, I was disappointed that the game puts a prominent highlight on every relevant piece of information you come across. Not only that, you even get direct notifications for cross-referenced sources, so basically you don't even have to read and remember anything. Sure, you make some interesting (but as I said, also pretty obvious) decisions about what to do with the tidbits, but it would be so much more fun and engaging if you actually had to identify the relevant puzzle pieces on your own. 

Maybe these mechanics are just there for the sake of convenience, but ultimately they make the sleuthing trivial, and that's a problem when combing through news/websites/chats *is* the gameplay.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is one of the few I don’t really feel I can fall down on either side. Ultimately, I felt I should mark it as unrecommended because I couldn’t bring myself to give it a thumbs up, and steam doesn’t have a ‘meh, its ok I guess’ option.

The story is, literally as it is titled, an Orwellian style, drama, I guess. Unfortunately the railroading detracts from the telling. 

The game play is actually pretty good and quite well done. As an investigator you’re expected to dig up as much information as you can regarding suspects in a terrorist attack, and then use their connections and the information gleaned to unpick what occurred and who is responsible, with the ultimate aim of preventing another attack. It is actually the limitations that are forced upon you to ensure you don’t get lost, combined with the multitude of ‘coincidences’ and other sloppy writing that only drives the story in a railroaded direction that bring the whole thing down.

Pros:
The game is easy to play, for the most part allows you to take your time reading the information and make your decision. The way the information is presented is also easy to digest and use. 
The characters are each unique and seem quite well thought out with their own motivations and histories. They also have an interesting dynamic that shows the growth, depth, and fading of their friendship as natural friendships have done.


Cons: 
The game opens with a single character to investigate, while that makes sense from a tutorial point, it doesn’t from a story point. This then focus and railroading leading to a contrived conclusion full of plot holes and excuses kinda ruins the game.
The system showcases a really interesting idea for ways to gather and profile information, monitor suspects, and use what you learn to further an investigation. Then it doesn’t let you do it, restricting what you can see to only a tiny window. It makes for a surveillance system that can’t watch anything.
Tying in to the above, we have so much information on the characters, but can’t utilise any of the information we would undoubtedly be able to access as law enforcement. Once again it felt like an artificial restriction, which was most frustrating.

Suggested improvements:
A skip dialogue button. Most of the few hours I’ve racked up were waiting for conversations to end.
Allow the system to access some of the surveyed individual’s data and build the puzzle environment that way.
Allow us to use the system in the ways we feel fit, not just the way that gives the narrative held.
For the love of god, let us investigate more people, more red herrings. Let us be the ones to cross off people from the lists, let us be the ones that decide what’s worth pursuing. 

Overall Recommendation:
This game has so much potential as a story driven and person centred hook. Especially for people who enjoy info hunts or detective style games. I can see it being really expandable with so many story options.
I think if you like that kind of game, this will scratch an itch for you.
But I can’t recommend it in its current state. As it is it comes off negatively and that just spoils all of the good things about it.

Entire chucks on the game where you do nothing but read exposition on a situation you have no emotional investment in.  This is my biggest contention with the game as intends to challenge the player's morality, but doesn't do so in a meaningful way (for me, at least).

Well made but it just won't scratch that bureaucratic, 'cog-in-the-machine' itch that you might be looking for, and in that regard I'm not too sure who this game is for.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell does one thing very well: it accurately simulates the tedium inherent in most government jobs. If you ever wanted to know what it's like to work at the DMV or IRS, Orwell is your game. The simplistic click-and-drag gameplay might have been mitigated by an interesting story or characters, but Orwell's plot is boilerplate paranoia fiction delivered in screen after screen of dull exposition. The puzzle design vacillates between the extremes of baffingly obtuse and blaringly obvious. At several points, I found myself simply clicking through every single screen and selecting every random bit of data I could simply to progress the story.

On the plus side, the ambient soundtrack is pleasant and includes the occasional dramatic sting to highlight twists in the storyline. The Orwell UI is clean and easy to navigate. I also think that the developers had the best of intentions to create a game that grapples with the rise of the surveillance state in modern societies.

Unfortunately, good intentions don't trump bad game design. Stay away from Borewell.

The game's got a very interesting premise and some cool ideas, but I think the execution falls flat - especially towards the end. My main problem - you're very limited in the sort of information that you can flag for the investigation. You can only pick pieces of texts, and their meaning in the investigation's context will be pre-decided. This was very annoying at the end - I figured out the main-man, the whodunit - but I couldn't incriminate them, the game didn't consider evidence that I inferred from as evidence. [spoiler] It's infuriating to see the bomber walk free when I tried to pick the morally good ending [/spoiler]

These game-mechanics just can't reflect the depth and complexity of a would-be mass-surveillance system, and the story and your choices have to bend to these limitations. Pick this up if you're interested - it is kinda thought provoking, but don't expect a cohesive story that reflects your choices well.

Basically, it's an interactive story founded on a great idea, but didn't meet its potential for me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise. In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time." Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest." Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!" When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon. Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good. The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that: ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer. You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision. As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed. Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility. On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise. By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.
